articles.summary: If you were a child of the early 1990s growing up in Kwara State, north central Nigeria, you had the rare privilege of making radio part of your life. In Shao, where I grew up, the migrant Hausa community was a huge radio community. Many Hausa people arrived in Kwara State from Kano to work on corn and okra fields, and in other types of farming. BBC Hausa and other radio stations provided them with essential international news and cultural programming. As for hardware, Kaito was popular, and so was Sony with its long antenna. Radio was culturally important to Shao in the Yoruba community as well. And I grew up under the foot of the old, who loved radio. My grandfather, who was blind, had an old President radio—a small Japanese model that ran on Tiger batteries. Most days, Abaja, my grandfather, had the radio on as his sole company. When he wanted to go out to visit his friend, I would help him navigate the boulders in front of our house. I grew up on this memory, but I remember too that I was glad to be at his side and help with his needs.
